ideas.text: Everything flows (panta rhei): 'You cannot step into the same river twice' — universal flux
Fire is the primordial element and the symbol of constant transformation in nature
The Logos is the rational principle governing the cosmos, accessible to reason but ignored by most
Opposites are united: 'The path up and down is one and the same' — unity of contraries
Strife (polemos) is the father of all things — conflict drives cosmic order and change
Being is; non-being is not — genuine change and plurality are impossible illusions
What is, is eternal, ungenerated, imperishable, indivisible, and complete — one and continuous
The Way of Truth (reason) vs. the Way of Opinion (sense perception) — only reason grasps reality
Zeno's paradoxes defend Parmenides by showing that assuming plurality leads to contradictions
Knowledge is virtue; ignorance is the source of evil — to know the good is to do it
The unexamined life is not worth living — philosophy as a way of life, not merely theory
True knowledge comes from recognizing one's own ignorance — Socratic intellectual humility
The soul is immortal and distinct from the body; care of the soul is paramount
The elenchus (Socratic method): knowledge emerges through dialectical questioning, not dogma
No one does evil willingly — wrongdoing stems from ignorance of what is truly good
The Theory of Forms: true reality consists of eternal, abstract, perfect Forms (eidos)
Knowledge is recollection (anamnesis) of what the soul knew before birth in the realm of Forms
The ideal state is ruled by philosopher-kings who have knowledge of the Good itself
The soul has three parts: reason (logos), spirit (thymos), and appetite (epithymia)
Justice is harmony between the parts of the soul and the classes of the state
The Allegory of the Cave: most humans see only shadows; philosophy liberates us into true light
The Form of the Good illuminates all other Forms like the sun illuminates visible things
Eros (love) is the soul's desire to ascend from beautiful bodies to Beauty itself
Poets and artists produce imitations of imitations — twice removed from truth
The Demiurge fashioned the cosmos from pre-existing matter using the Forms as a model
The divided line: reality has four levels — images, physical things, mathematical objects, Forms
Laws should be based on reason and aim at the common good of the whole community
Form and matter (hylemorphism) are inseparable; universals exist only in particular things
Knowledge begins with sensory experience; abstraction yields universal principles through induction
Eudaimonia (flourishing) is the highest human good, achieved through virtuous activity
Virtue (arete) is a mean between excess and deficiency — discovered by practical wisdom (phronesis)
Man is by nature a political animal (zoon politikon) — the polis exists by nature
Logic is the instrument (organon) of all sciences; syllogistic reasoning is the foundation of valid inference
Four causes explain change: material, formal, efficient, and final (teleological)
The unmoved mover (God) is pure actuality — the final cause that moves all things without being moved
Potentiality and actuality underlie all change and motion in nature
The best constitution mixes elements of monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy — polity
Tragedy achieves catharsis (purification) through pity and fear — art's ethical function
Friendship (philia) is essential to happiness and the binding force of communities
Natural slavery argument: some are by nature rulers, others by nature ruled (controversial)
Pleasure (ataraxia, freedom from disturbance) is the highest good and natural goal of life
The gods exist in perfect bliss but do not intervene in human affairs or cause events
Death is nothing to us: when we exist, death is absent; when death exists, we do not
Reality consists of atoms and void swerving unpredictably (clinamen) — basis of free will
Live according to nature and reason (logos); virtue is the only genuine good
We are all citizens of a cosmopolis — a universal community bound by shared reason
External things cannot harm the inner self; only our judgments about them can disturb us
The One (the Good) is the first principle beyond being, thought, and intelligibility — utterly simple
Emanation: from the One proceeds Intellect (Nous), then Soul, then the material world
The soul's return: through contemplative ascent, we can reunite with the One in mystical ecstasy
Matter is the lowest degree of reality — the principle of privation and darkness
God is the source of all truth; divine illumination makes knowledge possible for the mind
Evil is the privation (absence) of good, not a substance or independent force
Free will exists and is necessary for moral responsibility, though corrupted by original sin
Time exists only in the mind as distension (distentio); God exists outside time in eternal present
The heart is restless until it rests in God — human fulfillment lies only in divine love
Just war criteria: war must have just cause, legitimate authority, and right intention
Faith and reason are complementary paths to truth — grace does not destroy nature but perfects it
Five Ways (Quinque Viae): cosmological arguments demonstrating God's existence from motion, causation, contingency, gradation, and design
Natural law is grounded in divine reason and accessible to all through rational reflection
Essence and existence are really distinct in creatures — God alone is ipsum esse subsistens
Analogy of being: predicates applied to God and creatures are neither univocal nor equivocal but analogical
The cardinal virtues (prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance) are perfected by theological virtues (faith, hope, charity)
Ockham's Razor: do not multiply entities beyond necessity — simpler explanations are preferred
Nominalism: universals are names (flatus vocis), not real entities existing independently
Only individuals exist; all categories are mental constructs for organizing experience
Faith and reason are separate domains — theological truths cannot be proven by reason alone
The state of nature is a war of all against all — life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'
Social contract: individuals surrender rights to a sovereign (Leviathan) in exchange for security
Materialism: everything that exists is body in motion; mind is nothing but brain processes
Psychological egoism: all human actions are ultimately motivated by self-interest and fear of death
Cogito ergo sum: 'I think, therefore I am' — the indubitable foundation of all knowledge
Mind-body dualism: mind (res cogitans) and body (res extensa) are two distinct substances
Clear and distinct ideas perceived by natural light of reason are guaranteed true by a non-deceiving God
Ontological argument: God's essence necessarily entails existence — the supremely perfect being must exist
Methodic doubt: doubt everything possible to find what cannot be doubted — foundationalism
Animals are automata — they lack rational souls and thus consciousness
The pineal gland is the point of interaction between immaterial mind and material body
Primary qualities (extension, shape, motion) are objective; secondary qualities (color, taste) depend on perceivers
Pascal's Wager: believing in God is pragmatically rational since infinite gain outweighs finite loss
The heart has its reasons which reason knows not — intuitive understanding exceeds logic
Human condition: we are between the infinitely large and small — wretched yet capable of greatness
The order of heart vs. the order of reason: different domains require different methods
God or Nature (Deus sive Natura) — only one substance exists; pantheistic monism
Mind and body are two attributes of the same substance — parallelism without causal interaction
Freedom is acting in accordance with one's own nature and necessity — understanding leads to blessedness
Adequate ideas (rational understanding) free us from passive emotions and external determination
Intellectual love of God (amor Dei intellectualis) — the highest human happiness through intuitive knowledge
Emotions arise from inadequate ideas; understanding their causes allows mastery over them
Democracy is the most natural form of government — it expresses individual freedom within collective reason
The mind is a tabula rasa (blank slate) at birth — all knowledge originates in experience
Natural rights: every person has inherent rights to life, liberty, and property
Government legitimacy rests on the consent of the governed — right of revolution against tyranny
Primary qualities (shape, solidity, motion) inhere in objects; secondary qualities (color, taste) depend on perception
Personal identity consists in psychological continuity of consciousness over time
Toleration: the state has no authority over the inner religious beliefs of its citizens
Monads: reality consists of infinitely many simple, indivisible, windowless spiritual substances
This is the best of all possible worlds — God chose it among infinities for maximum variety and harmony
Pre-established harmony: monads do not causally interact but are synchronized by God at creation
Innate ideas: the mind contains truths and tendencies from reason, not blank like a tablet
Identity of indiscernibles: no two things can share exactly the same properties
Sufficient reason: nothing happens without a reason why it should be so rather than otherwise
'Esse est percipi': to be is to be perceived — objects consist entirely of perceptions
Matter does not exist independently — only minds and their ideas (immaterialism/subjective idealism)
God perceives all things continuously — this guarantees objective existence when no finite mind observes
Abstract general ideas are impossible — we only ever perceive particular, concrete instances
Separation of powers (executive, legislative, judicial) is essential to prevent tyranny
Laws must be adapted to the people, climate, and customs of each nation — legal relativism
Despotism is ruled by fear; monarchy by honor; republic by virtue
Commerce promotes peace and tolerance between nations
All knowledge derives from impressions (vivid sensations) and ideas (faint copies) — radical empiricism
Causation is a habit of the mind formed by constant conjunction, not necessary connection in nature
The self is a bundle of perceptions — there is no underlying substantial self behind experience
Moral judgments express sentiment (passions), not reason — reason is the slave of the passions
The problem of induction: no rational justification exists for inferring the future from the past
Miracles are inherently improbable — testimony cannot overcome the weight of uniform experience
Is-ought gap: one cannot derive normative ('ought') statements purely from descriptive ('is') statements
Free will and determinism are compatible (compatibilism) — liberty is acting according to one's desires
Man is naturally good (bon sauvage); society, private property, and civilization corrupt him
The Social Contract: legitimate political authority arises from the general will (volonté générale) of the people
Natural inequality is acceptable; social inequality of power and wealth is artificial and unjust
Private property is the origin of civil society and also of inequality and conflict
General will aims at the common good; it differs from the will of all (sum of private interests)
Education should follow nature's pace — nurture innate goodness rather than impose conformity
Copernican revolution: the mind actively structures experience — space, time, and categories are a priori forms
Phenomena (things as they appear) vs. noumena (things-in-themselves) — we know only appearances
Categorical Imperative: act only according to maxims you could will as universal laws
Moral worth depends solely on acting from duty (good will), never on inclination or consequences
Humanity formula: treat humanity (yourself and others) always as an end, never merely as means
Autonomy of the will: moral law is self-legislation by rational beings — true freedom is obedience to reason
Kingdom of ends: a systematic union of rational beings through common moral laws
The sublime: aesthetic experience of overwhelming magnitude (mathematical) or power (dynamic) that exceeds comprehension
Perpetual peace: republics with democratic constitutions tend toward peace — foundations of liberal internationalism
Antinomies of pure reason: reason inevitably produces contradictory conclusions about the cosmos, freedom, and God
Enlightenment motto: 'Sapere aude!' — dare to think for yourself, emerge from self-imposed immaturity
Teleological judgment: we must regard organisms as if designed by purpose, though this remains regulative not constitutive
Postulates of practical practical reason: God, freedom, and immortality are necessary presuppositions of morality
Absolute Spirit (Geist) unfolds itself through history — reality is dynamic, rational process
Dialectic: every concept contains its own negation; thesis-antithesis-synthesis drives all development
Freedom is realized through ethical life (Sittlichkeit): family, civil society, and constitutional state
Master-slave dialectic: self-consciousness requires recognition by another — struggle for recognition shapes history
'What is rational is actual, and what is actual is rational' — philosophy understands what already is
World-historical individuals (Napoleon etc.) advance Spirit's development through their unconscious passions
Art, religion, and philosophy are three modes of Absolute Spirit's self-understanding — philosophy is highest
The cunning of reason: individuals pursue private ends but unintentionally realize reason's larger plan
The World as Will and Representation: the noumenal reality is blind, striving Will; phenomenal reality is Representation
Will-to-live is the fundamental drive behind all existence — the source of endless suffering
Aesthetic contemplation (especially music) offers temporary escape from the tyranny of the Will
Compassion (Mitleid) is the basis of ethics — recognizing the same suffering Will in others
Denial of the Will through asceticism is the path to liberation and peace (Nirvana-like)
Pessimism: life is more suffering than pleasure; non-existence would be preferable
Utilitarianism refined: maximize happiness (quality matters, not just quantity) for all affected sentient beings
Higher pleasures (intellectual, moral, aesthetic) are qualitatively superior to lower (bodily) pleasures
Harm Principle: individual liberty may only be restricted to prevent harm to others — foundation of classical liberalism
Freedom of thought and expression: even false opinions must be protected — truth emerges from open contest
Induction by enumeration: enumerative induction grounded in uniformity of nature (vs. Whewell's hypothetico-deductive)
Three stages of existence: aesthetic (pleasure), ethical (duty), and religious (faith) — qualitative leaps between them
Subjectivity is truth: truth is not objective but involves passionate inward commitment of the individual
Leap of faith: belief in the absurd (like Abraham's sacrifice) transcends rational justification
Either/Or: life demands decisive choice — refusing to choose is itself a despairing choice
Despair (sygdom til døden) is the sickness unto death: not willing to be oneself
Irony (after Socrates) exposes contradictions in systems and clears ground for authentic existence
Historical materialism: history is driven by class struggle rooted in material/economic conditions of production
Alienation: capitalism separates workers from their labor, products, species-being, and other humans
Base and superstructure: economic relations shape ideology, law, culture, and religion
Communism: goal of a classless society where each contributes according to ability, receives according to need
Labor theory of value: the value of commodities is determined by socially necessary labor time
Dictatorship of the proletariat: transitional state where workers seize and hold power before classlessness
Religion is the opium of the people — it masks real exploitation and promises illusory consolation
Pragmatic Maxim: the meaning of a conception lies in its conceivable practical effects
Semiotics: signs consist of object, representamen, and interpretant — triadic relation underlies all meaning
Abduction (retroduction): inference to the best explanation — the logical form of hypothesis generation
Fallibilism: no belief is absolutely certain — inquiry is an endless community process of correction
Three categories of being: Firstness (quality), Secondness (reaction), Thirdness (representation/mediation)
Pragmatic theory of truth: truth is what works in practice — ideas are verified by their experiential consequences
Radical empiricism: both relations and terms are directly experienced — neutral monism of pure experience
Stream of consciousness: thought is continuous, flowing, and personal — never discrete fragments
The will to believe: in genuinely live, forced, momentous options, faith-based choice is permissible
Pluralistic universe: reality is unfinished, containing genuine novelty and multiple independent realities
'God is dead': traditional absolute values collapse — we face nihilism in modernity
Will to Power (Wille zur Macht): the fundamental drive underlying all life and becoming
Eternal Recurrence: the ultimate affirmation test — would you will to live this identical life infinitely?
Übermensch (Overman): create new values beyond slave/master morality — self-overcoming
Master morality (good/bad: noble/powerful) vs. slave morality (good/evil: weak/resentful)
Amor fati: love your fate — affirm all of life, including suffering and pain, unconditionally
Perspectivism: there are no facts, only interpretations — all knowledge is from particular standpoints
Critique of truth: truth is a mobile army of metaphors — useful fictions become solidified as 'truth'
Revaluation of all values: transvalue decadent values (pity, equality) into life-affirming ones
Apollo vs. Dionysus: Greek tragedy combines Apollonian form/order with Dionysian chaos/ecstasy
Logicism: arithmetic (and mathematics) is reducible to logic — numbers are logical objects
Sense (Sinn) and reference (Bedeutung): expressions have both meaning (mode of presentation) and referent
Thoughts (propositions/Gedanken) are objective, timeless, abstract entities — not mental states
Modern predicate calculus: invented quantifiers (∀, ∃) and formalized logical notation
Instrumentalism: thinking is an instrument for solving problems arising from organism-environment interaction
Learning by doing: education is growth through experience — not preparation for future life but life itself
Democracy as a way of life: participatory community where individuals freely develop through cooperative association
Inquiry begins with a felt difficulty and ends with resolved situation — the pattern of reflective thought
The public and its problems: democracy must adapt to technological society through expanded communication
Intentionality: all consciousness is consciousness OF something — the defining feature of mental states
Epoché (phenomenological reduction): bracket the natural attitude to examine pure phenomena as given
Go back to the things themselves: describe experience exactly as it appears, prior to theories and explanations
Lifeworld (Lebenswelt): the pre-theoretical world of everyday experience that science presupposes but cannot replace
Transcendental phenomenology: investigate the conditions of possibility of experience itself
Intersubjectivity: the Other is constituted in experience — solipsism is overcome through empathetic apprehension
Logical atomism: the world consists of atomic facts mirrored by elementary propositions in language
Knowledge by acquaintance (direct awareness) vs. knowledge by description (definite descriptions)
Theory of definite descriptions: analyze 'The F is G' using quantifiers and predication — eliminate denoting phrases
Logicism (with Whitehead in Principia Mathematica): reduce mathematics to pure logic
Inference of other minds: analogy from observed behavior to inferred mental states (argument from analogy)
Early: The world is the totality of facts, not things — language pictures atomic facts (picture theory)
Early: Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent — limits of language = limits of thought
Later: Meaning is use — words mean nothing outside their role in language-games embedded in forms of life
Later: Philosophy as therapy — dissolve pseudo-problems caused by bewitchment of intelligence by language
Later: Private language is impossible — rule-following requires publicly checkable criteria
Family resemblance: concepts need no single essence; members overlap like family faces
Language-games: countless distinct activities governed by rules — no underlying essence to 'language'
Form of life: meaning is grounded in shared practices, customs, and forms of activity
Rule-following paradox: no course of action can be determined by a rule alone — interpretation always underdetermined
Certainty: some propositions (like 'Here is a hand') are hinges on which all doubt and inquiry turn
Dasein (being-there): human existence is always already being-in-the-world — not a subject observing an object
Being-toward-death (Sein zum Tod): authentic existence requires owning one's finitude and individual mortality
The question of Being (Seinsfrage): Western metaphysics has forgotten the difference between beings and Being itself
Technology (Gestell): modern enframing reveals the world as standing-reserve — danger to authentic dwelling
Authenticity (Eigentlichkeit): owning one's thrownness, choosing oneself amid fallenness into das Man (the They)
Care (Sorge): Dasein's fundamental structure — ahead-of-itself, already-being-in, alongside entities
Hermeneutic phenomenology: interpret (not just describe) Dasein's being because Dasein is self-interpreting
Poetry as privileged site of unconcealedness (Aletheia): art reveals what technology conceals
Falsifiability: demarcation criterion — scientific theories must be potentially falsifiable by observation
Conjectures and refutations: science progresses by bold conjectures followed by rigorous attempts to falsify
Open Society: oppose totalitarianism and historicist grand narratives that claim inevitable progress
Critical rationalism: hold all beliefs provisionally — remain perpetually open to revision and criticism
Existence precedes essence: humans first exist, then define themselves through choices — no fixed nature
Radical freedom: we are 'condemned to be free' — absolutely responsible for all we choose and refuse
Bad faith (mauvaise foi): self-deception that denies our freedom and responsibility
Look (regard): encountering another's gaze objectifies me — others threaten my freedom
Being-for-itself vs. being-in-itself: consciousness is pure negation and lack; things are full positivity
Banality of evil: great evil can be committed by ordinary people through thoughtless obedience, not monstrous malice
Vita activa: three modes of human activity — labor (biological), work (fabrication), action (political/speech)
Natality: each human birth represents new beginning and capacity to initiate the unprecedented
Totalitarianism: uses terror and ideology to create atomized masses — fundamentally different from tyranny
The right to have rights: belonging to a political community is prerequisite for having any rights at all
Body-subject (corps propre): the body is not an object but our primary way of being in the world
Perception is embodied: we perceive through our bodily engagement, not detached observation
Ambiguity of perception: meaning is always incomplete, situated, and open-ended — against Cartesian clarity
Chiasm: reversibility of touching/being touched — subject and object intertwine in bodily experience
Two Dogmas of Empiricism: reject analytic/synthetic distinction and reductionism — holistic web of belief
Holism (confirmation holism): statements face the tribunal of experience as a body, not individually
Naturalized epistemology: epistemology is a chapter of psychology — study how humans actually form beliefs
Indeterminacy of translation: multiple incompatible translation manuals between languages are equally empirically adequate
Ontological relativity: there is no privileged reference frame — ontology relative to background language
Anomalous monism: mental events are identical with physical events but have no strict psychophysical laws
Principle of charity: we must assume most of a speaker's beliefs are true to interpret them at all
Triangulation: thought, language, and knowledge require interaction between two creatures and a shared world
Radical interpretation: understanding a language requires simultaneously interpreting beliefs and meanings
Justice as fairness: principles of justice chosen from behind a veil of ignorance (original position)
Difference Principle: social and economic inequalities are just only if they benefit the least advantaged
Reflective equilibrium: balance considered moral intuitions with principled moral theory
Two principles: (1) equal basic liberties for all, (2) fair equality of opportunity + difference principle
Overlapping consensus: pluralistic societies can agree on political principles despite differing comprehensive doctrines
Paradigm shifts: science progresses through revolutionary breaks, not smooth cumulative accumulation
Normal science: puzzle-solving within accepted paradigm until anomalies accumulate and trigger crisis
Incommensurability: paradigms cannot be fully translated into each other — scientists inhabit different worlds
Power/knowledge: power and knowledge are inseparable — each regime of truth enables and hides forms of power
Discourse constructs its objects — what counts as madness, sexuality, or illness varies historically
Disciplinary power: modern institutions (prisons, schools, hospitals) produce docile bodies through surveillance
Biopower: modern states govern populations through regulation of life processes (birth, health, mortality)
Archaeology of knowledge: analyze historical conditions that make certain statements possible/thinkable
The author is a function: texts produce authors, not vice versa — decenter the creative subject
Communicative action: rationality resides in reaching understanding through undistorted speech, not instrumental success
Ideal speech situation: discourse free from coercion where the better argument alone prevails
Public sphere: space of rational-critical debate between state and civil society — endangered by media and capital
Discourse ethics: moral norms are valid only if all affected could consent as participants in practical discourse
Deconstruction: expose how texts undermine their own claimed meanings through internal contradictions
Différance: meaning is endlessly deferred through chains of signifiers — never fully present
Logocentrism critique: Western thought privileges speech over writing and presence over absence
There is nothing outside the text (il n'y a pas de hors-texte): all interpretation is textual
Ethics of hospitality: unconditional welcome of the Other — justice is always to-come, never achieved
The Chinese Room: syntax manipulation is not sufficient for semantics — computation is not understanding
Speech acts: language is not just describing reality but performing actions (asserting, promising, commanding)
Biological naturalism: consciousness is a biological phenomenon caused by brain processes
Social reality: institutional facts (money, marriage, property) depend on collective intentionality
The minimal state: only functions needed to protect against force, theft, fraud, and enforce contracts
Entitlement theory: justice in holdings depends on just acquisition and voluntary transfer
Taxation of earnings from labor is on a par with forced labor
The Utility Monster: if a being gets enormously more utility from resources, utilitarianism would sacrifice everyone else
All sentient beings deserve equal consideration of interests — speciesism is morally wrong
Preference utilitarianism: maximize the satisfaction of preferences of all affected beings
Effective altruism: we should donate to causes that do the most good per dollar spent
Famine, Affluence, and Morality: if we can prevent suffering without sacrificing anything comparable, we must
